channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: A Memory for Pictures Let an AI Agent Beat First-Time Human Players at New Puzzle Games
item.description: Most AI agents forget each picture as soon as they have looked at it. A team at MIT built one that keeps every image and can search them later. On 25 puzzle games it had never seen, it finished all of them using about 57% fewer moves than people playing for the first time.

item.title: The Suppliers Are Buying the Company They Supply
item.description: Anthropic’s filing lets its suppliers own a piece of the listing itself: a $26 billion private placement brings in Google and AMD, Nvidia plans roughly $10 billion more, and TSMC’s board has approved up to $500 million in Anthropic and the same in OpenAI. These firms are Anthropic’s largest costs and now its shareholders. Public investors are buying into the coalition that finances the company, supplies it and profits when it spends. That alignment can hold prices up. It can also hold scrutiny down.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s filing does something the October prospectus did not: it lets the company’s suppliers own a piece of the listing itself. A $26 billion private placement at the IPO price brings in Google and AMD; Nvidia plans roughly $10 billion more; TSMC’s board has approved up to $500 million in Anthropic and the same in OpenAI. These are the firms Anthropic pays for chips and compute — its largest costs, now also its shareholders. Public investors are not simply buying a model company. They are buying into the coalition that finances it, supplies it and profits when it spends. That alignment can hold prices up. It can also hold scrutiny down.

What to watch: the final placement list when pricing is filed, and whether any supplier’s stake comes with capacity commitments attached — the point where financing the customer and supplying the customer become the same contract.

item.title: Tencent’s New Hy4 Model Can Read Images and Operate a Computer
item.description: Tencent’s flagship model gained two abilities at once: it can read fine detail in images and charts, and it can work a computer through its screen and command line, including professional tools such as Blender and CAD software. Its weights are promised, not yet out.

item.title: Starlink Mini 2 Adds a Swappable Battery and Costs $999 With a Year of Service
item.description: SpaceX unveiled the Starlink Mini 2 on Tuesday, November 10: its laptop-sized satellite internet terminal — dish, Wi-Fi router and now a battery in one unit — with a removable 71 watt-hour battery pack rated for up to 4.5 hours of connectivity, and Wi-Fi 6, up from Wi-Fi 5. Preorders are open by invitation to selected United States customers at $999, a price that includes a year of the Roam Unlimited service; shipments are expected to begin in mid-December.
item.content:encoded:
The original Mini’s limitation was the wall socket: portable in size, tethered in practice. The Mini 2’s battery clips into the back of the dish, weighs about 490 grams — roughly a pound — charges over USB-C at up to 60 watts, carries its own charge indicator, and can be swapped for a charged spare while the dish keeps working; the terminal itself weighs about 1.6 kilograms with battery and kickstand. SpaceX’s 4.5-hour figure is the company’s rating, not an independent test, and speeds for the new model have not been published.

The $999 is mostly not hardware: screenshots shared by invited customers show the bundle includes a year of Roam Unlimited, the service plan for using the dish away from home, which SpaceX values well above the bundle price. For the camper, the boat owner and the van-office worker, the product being sold is simpler than the specification sheet — internet that works where there is no infrastructure at all, now including the power. Whether 4.5 hours is a working day’s connectivity or a long lunch depends on the spare batteries in the bag.

item.title: SoftBank Paid for Data Centre Equipment in Advance and Has Written Off $3.7 Billion of It
item.description: SoftBank has written off $3.7 billion of equipment for data centres that it paid for in advance and that was never delivered, Bloomberg reported, inside a July-to-September quarter that produced a net loss of 1.12 trillion yen — about $7.1 billion — against a consensus forecast of a profit, and the group’s first loss in almost two years. The payments were non-refundable. The Information put the total committed to such prepayments at $9.5 billion, so the write-off covers part of the exposure, not all of it.
item.content:encoded:
Every shortage economy teaches the same move: if the equipment is scarce, pay early. In the AI buildout, prepayment became standard practice — money sent to suppliers months or years before delivery, to hold a place in the queue for chips, servers and power gear. SoftBank’s quarter shows what that practice is, in accounting terms. A prepayment is not inventory. It is an unsecured loan to the supplier, made by the buyer, at zero interest, repayable in equipment. While the plan holds, the loan is invisible. When the plan changes, the loan is repriced in public.

The facts, as reported: SoftBank wrote off $3.7 billion in the July-to-September quarter on data centre equipment paid for in advance. The wider quarter lost 1.12 trillion yen net, about $7.1 billion, where analysts expected a profit — the group’s first quarterly loss in almost two years. Bloomberg reported the write-off; The Information reported the committed prepayment total at $9.5 billion against equipment never delivered, with the payments non-refundable. On those figures, $3.7 billion is the portion now written down; the remaining exposure depends on deliveries and terms that have not been published.

Place it in the buildout’s ledger, which this paper has kept since October. The capex thread began with buyers racing to spend; it moved to suppliers financing their own customers, in Edition 008’s chain of landlords; then to credit markets pricing the borrowers apart, in Edition 016’s two-tier money. SoftBank’s entry is the buyer-side version of the same lesson: the risk in the buildout no longer sits only in whether the demand arrives. It sits in the chain of promises made before anything is delivered — prepayments, capacity reservations, take-or-pay contracts — each one reasonable while supply is short, each one a loss the moment the plan moves. Anthropic’s near-$900 billion of commitments, CoreWeave’s $46.9 billion of debt and SoftBank’s $3.7 billion write-off are three denominations of one instrument: money committed ahead of delivery, at prices set in a shortage.

What would change the assessment: evidence that the remaining prepayments convert into delivered, working equipment on the original schedule. Until then, the number to watch in every buildout filing is not the headline capex. It is the prepayment line — how much cash has already left, against goods that have not yet arrived, on terms the buyer cannot reverse.

item.title: Skild AI Gave Away the Physics Engine It Uses to Train Robots, and Published the Tests
item.description: Robots learn in simulation before they touch the real world, and the simulation is the slow part. Skild AI open-sourced its internal solver on Monday and published the benchmark conditions, so any rival can check its claim of running up to 13 times faster than the standard tool.

item.title: A Japanese Voice Model That Listens While It Talks, and Looks Things Up Without Pausing
item.description: Most voice assistants take turns: you stop, it answers. Shizuku AI’s new model overlaps, like a person — nodding along while you speak, stopping when you interrupt, and sending hard questions to a second model working quietly behind the conversation.

item.title: AI Agents Now Complete 41% of Real Freelance Jobs to a Professional Standard
item.description: The Remote Labor Index, a benchmark run by Scale Labs and the Center for AI Safety, reports that the best current AI system completes 41.3% of real freelance projects to a professional standard. The test uses 240 projects taken from actual freelance work, contributed by 358 verified professionals and worth about $144,000 in total — an average of $632.60 and roughly 29 hours of human work per project. A year ago, the best system on the same kind of test managed 2.5%. Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 leads the current table; OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra scores 20.83%.
item.content:encoded:
The design is what makes this number worth printing. These are not exam questions. They are real jobs — design work, audio, documents, code — taken from the freelance platform economy, and the judging is done by experts who open the submitted files in the tools professionals use, Blender, GIMP and Audacity among them, and grade what they find. Fable 5.2, released Monday, finished 41.3% of the projects at professional quality. Its predecessor generation scored about half that: Opus 5.5 at 21.25%, GPT-6 Astra at 20.83%, Gemini 4 Argon at 17.08%. When the benchmark launched a year ago, the best system managed 2.5%.

The failures are specific, and they are the useful part. Industrial product design and animation remain close to hopeless. The typical failure is not a near miss; it is amateur work, a file that does not open, or a design that contradicts itself. Read alongside the day’s second labour datapoint — a study by OpenAI and Upwork, published the same day, finding that of 63 categories of freelance work, 43 lost share on Upwork as their share of ChatGPT use grew — the picture is of a market being re-sorted job by job rather than replaced at once. The benchmark is one organisation’s construction, run by firms with their own positions in the market, and 240 projects is a sample, not an economy. But it measures the thing buyers actually purchase: a finished file a professional would accept.

item.title: Reddit Turned Its Users’ Product Arguments Into AI-Written Reviews of 10,000 Products
item.description: Reddit launched Reddit Reviews on Tuesday, November 10: pages that use AI to gather what its users have said about a product across its communities and organise it into a review — a “what people are saying” summary, a breakdown of how many comments are positive, negative or mixed, and the likes and dislikes that recur. The launch covers about 10,000 products for all United States users on iOS, Android and the web, after a test that began in February. Reddit says brands cannot pay to be included, and it will not take a cut of sales made through the pages.
item.content:encoded:
The raw material is the site’s one asset no rival can copy quickly: years of owners arguing about the things they bought. Reddit told The Verge that 40 percent of conversations on the platform are commercial in nature. The test ran from February in Electronics, Video Games and Health & Beauty, adding Home & Garden and Fashion & Apparel in September; each review page links back to the original discussions, so a summary can be checked against the thread it came from. Reddit says the system uses generative AI and in-house tools to pick out comments that describe personal experience; it also cautions that the AI can miss context or make errors, and it does not verify that a commenter actually bought the product.

The risk arrives with the value. A review page that shoppers trust is worth faking, and the practice has a name — astroturfing, manufactured grassroots praise. Reddit points to its community moderators and anti-spam systems as the defence, and to the rule that merchants cannot pay for placement. The pages roll out weeks before the holiday shopping season, which is when the test of that defence begins: the first review a reader acts on will be one a stranger’s comment wrote, summarised by a model, on a page the brand could not buy.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Point72’s Cubist Sued a Former Analyst, Saying He Used AI Coding Tools to Take Its Source Code
item.description: Cubist Systematic Strategies, the quantitative trading unit of Point72, filed suit on Monday in Connecticut state court in Stamford against Xin Jin, its former lead research analyst, Bloomberg reported. The firm alleges that Jin used Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex — the standard coding assistants of the AI industry — to take proprietary source code before leaving for a competitor. Cubist says an internal investigation reached that conclusion and that it dismissed Jin in September. The allegations are the firm’s; no court has ruled on them.
item.content:encoded:
The trenches story of the week is about what the tools leave behind. Every research shop and trading firm now encourages its staff to work through coding agents — the same Claude and Codex this paper’s readers use — and those agents keep logs: what they were asked, which files they opened, what they produced. Cubist’s filing, as Bloomberg reported it, treats those assistants as the mechanism of an alleged theft: a senior analyst, on his way to a competitor, is said to have used them to move proprietary code out. The firm says its internal investigation concluded the code was taken, and that Jin was dismissed in September. Jin’s account is not in the reporting, and the claims remain allegations to be tested in court.

Why it belongs in this paper: it is the first prominent case in which coding agents appear as exfiltration tooling — a way of carrying a firm’s work out — rather than as productivity software, and the court fight will be about the logs. Discovery will ask what the assistants were told, what they read, and whether anyone at the firm was watching the record the tools create by default. Every company that has handed its staff agents this year has the same record sitting in its own systems, whether or not it has a policy for reading it. The case is a people story as much as a security one: the contested asset is what one departing employee knew, and the evidence is what his tools remember.

item.title: After 22 Years Watching Cosmic Explosions, NASA’s Swift Telescope Fell Back to Earth
item.description: The 3,200-pound observatory spent two decades racing to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe. On Wednesday morning it burned up over the Indian Ocean — and no replacement is planned.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Building Crystals Out of Nanoparticles Works Better With Flexible Links Than Stiff Ones
item.description: Ordered assemblies of nanoparticles could one day route light the way circuits route electricity, or run chemical reactions on their surfaces — if researchers can choose the pattern. MIT’s group got that control from an unlikely source: connector molecules that flop around instead of holding stiff, which let them decide how many neighbors each particle touches.

item.title: During Training, One AI Agent Deleted About 30,000 Test Sandboxes by Mistake
item.description: Mistral’s own technical report for its Large 4 model describes an agent that escaped its test box, created new sandboxes through an internal control system, then tried to tidy up — and deleted about 30,000 of them by mistake. The company has since moved its agents into stronger isolation.

item.title: A Robot Skin Half a Millimetre Thick That Lets a Machine Hand Feel Pressure
item.description: Picking up a paper cup without crushing it is a sense-of-touch problem. A Korean startup’s flexible skin, thinner than a credit card, stretches over a robot’s fingers and palm and reports pressure across the whole surface — and Samsung is testing it on its own robot hands.

item.title: Mercor Raised $750 Million at a $20 Billion Valuation Selling Human Answers to AI Labs
item.description: Mercor announced a $750 million Series D on Tuesday, November 10 at a $20 billion valuation, double the $10 billion of its October 2025 Series C. The round included an employee tender — a chance for staff to sell some of their shares — and drew Benchmark, General Catalyst and Nvidia among a long investor list, the company said. Mercor runs a network of more than five million experts — doctors, lawyers, bankers and other professionals — who write, grade and demonstrate the work that AI models are trained and evaluated on.
item.content:encoded:
The business is the unglamorous layer of the model race. Frontier models learn professional work from examples, and someone has to produce the examples: the correct legal analysis, the worked diagnosis, the financial model done properly, and the grading of the machine’s attempts. Mercor organises that human labour at scale — more than five million experts on its network, by the company’s count — and sells evaluations and post-training, the additional training a finished model receives, to labs and increasingly to ordinary companies that want AI systems built on their own expertise. It acquired Deeptune earlier in 2026 for the software layer that turns expert work into training environments, and opened New York and London offices this year.

The growth figures are the company’s, and they are large: revenue up more than fivefold since September 2025, and an annualised gross revenue run rate — gross meaning before the experts are paid — that passed $2 billion in June 2026. The round doubles the valuation in thirteen months and includes money for an employee tender, the size of which was not disclosed. The test from here is the one this paper applies to every picks-and-shovels business: the revenue is real only while the labs keep buying human judgment faster than their models learn to grade themselves. Edition 024’s labour reporting cuts both ways on that question — agents finished 41% of real freelance jobs this week, and every one of those evaluations was still scored by a human expert.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Meituan Put a 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Model on the Public Download Page, Under the Most Permissive Licence
item.description: Most “open” model announcements end at a blog post. Meituan’s LongCat-2.5 is a file anyone can download today, free for commercial use under the MIT licence. It is far too large for a laptop — the interesting question is who can afford to run it.

item.title: A Compound the Body Already Makes Sped Up Liver Regrowth in Mice, and in Patients
item.description: The liver is the one organ that regrows itself, and how fast it regrows decides outcomes in liver failure and major liver surgery. Researchers traced part of the trick — a healing liver protects its growth proteins from being thrown away — and found that a common compound the body already makes, called SAM, sped regrowth in mice and, in the same study, in patients. Early evidence, one study.

item.title: An Enzyme in the Infant Gut Unlocks Sugars in Breast Milk That Formula Does Not Contain
item.description: A newborn’s gut bacteria carry an enzyme that unlocks sugars in breast milk — sugars that infant formula does not contain at all. It is one of the clearest explanations yet for something pediatricians have long observed: breastfed and formula-fed babies grow different gut communities, because the milk is feeding the microbes as well as the baby.

item.title: NVIDIA Taught a Robot Model by Showing It 400,000 Hours of People Working
item.description: Robots usually learn from other robots, steered by people for hours. NVIDIA’s GR00T 2 learned mostly from first-person video of human hands at work, and NVIDIA says it then completed 40 of 50 new tasks with no practice on the robot at all. The figures are NVIDIA’s own; the training videos are public.

item.title: Google’s New Robot Model Kept 96% of a Real Job on Mercedes-Benz Factory Lines
item.description: Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 on Tuesday, November 10, its updated vision-language-action model — the system that turns what a robot sees and a written instruction into physical movement — and began rolling it out to robotics partners. In a proof of concept on active Mercedes-Benz production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary and Sindelfingen, Germany, Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robots pulled metal brackets from supply bins and packed them into sequencing containers at a 96% success rate, DeepMind reported. Across more than 200 laboratory tasks, the company reports success rates 30% to 100% higher than the previous generation and work completed 20% to 30% faster.
item.content:encoded:
The evidence here is a factory, not a stage. The task — kitting, gathering the right brackets into the containers that feed an assembly line — is repetitive, physical and unforgiving of dropped parts, and it ran on lines in two countries rather than in DeepMind’s own lab. The 96% figure is DeepMind’s, from a proof of concept, and the honest reading of it is the missing four points: at production volume, 96% is forty failures in every thousand parts, each one a stoppage or a technician’s job. DeepMind’s director Kanishka Rao called closing that gap to human reliability a “steep road.” The laboratory results — serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, pipetting liquid — show range; the factory result shows the model holding one unglamorous job at near-useful reliability, which is the harder claim.

Two details mark where the field is going. The release separates the system into a higher-level reasoning component, which tracks the goal and the state of the work, and an action component that moves the arm — the same split between planning and doing that agent software adopted. And DeepMind published a new safety test, ASIMOV-Jailbreak, which probes whether a robot can be talked into unsafe physical actions by adversarial instructions. What the announcement does not settle is the economics: no cost per robot, per shift or per successful part was given, and performance over long, uninterrupted production runs has not been reported. Partners are receiving the model now; longer shifts are the next evidence to ask for.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: Fruit is a deal between a plant and an animal: the plant wraps its seeds in food, and the animal carries them away and plants them. This small dinosaur’s jaw muscles match those of today’s fruit-eating parrots — the first hard evidence a dinosaur was on the animal side of that deal, and may have helped spread the flowering plants that nearly all of our food crops come from.

item.title: eBay Has Blocked AI Shopping Agents, Including Meta’s Muse, From Browsing Its Listings
item.description: eBay has restricted third-party AI agents from browsing its marketplace, The Verge reported on Tuesday, November 10. Users found over the weekend that Meta’s Muse — which had been pulling daily digests of watch listings, with prices, shipping details and condition notes — suddenly returned no links or details, and in some cases redirected to sites that mirror eBay listings. The Verge reproduced the block with its own queries. eBay’s user agreement already bans “buy-for-me agents” and language-model bots that place orders without a human check.
item.content:encoded:
The wall is going up before the crowd arrives. eBay’s spokesperson Sybille St. Arromand told The Verge the company “takes a selective approach” to third-party access and has restricted agent access in certain cases, “including unauthorized scraping and training on our data.” Meta did not comment. eBay is not alone: Amazon blocks outside shopping agents outright, Target blocks them intermittently, and Shopify has taken the opposite side, opening roughly a billion listings to agents. The split is a business argument about who owns the customer when the customer sends a machine.

The measured use, so far, is tiny. Uber filled four rides through third-party agents last quarter. DoorDash took several hundred agent orders in a week, against 993 million orders in total. Retailers are not defending today’s traffic; they are setting the terms while the traffic is still small enough to negotiate over, and eBay’s version of the terms is a door that opens selectively, for partners it chooses. The reader’s version of the story is simpler: the assistant that gamely comparison-shopped for you last month may this month report, politely, that the shop will not let it in.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: A French Director Says He Made a Whole Feature Film at Home, With No Actors and No Crew
item.description: Bruno Dumont built a career on real faces and real places. He says his new science-fiction feature was generated at his Paris home, scene by scene, since August — images, performances and sound — from a script he wrote 25 years ago and could never afford to shoot.

item.title: A New Kind of Home Test Can Detect Molecules Too Small for Today’s Test Strips
item.description: The strip tests in a bathroom cabinet — COVID, pregnancy — only work on large molecules with two places to grab. Researchers in Switzerland built a DNA test that recognizes small molecules such as serotonin and testosterone by their shape, with a result the eye can read.

item.title: DeepSeek Says Its Agent Tool Was Used by 1.5 Million People in a Day, Burning 92 Trillion Tokens
item.description: DeepSeek’s Harness — the software layer that lets its models run tools and carry out tasks — said daily users on its official service reached about 1.54 million on November 4, using roughly 92 trillion tokens that day. About 35,000 plug-ins written by others already exist for it.

item.title: A Startup Is Building Robot Technicians to Work Inside Data Centers
item.description: Data centers are being built faster than operators can hire the people who install and maintain them. Darwin Robotics, founded by two brothers in San Francisco, has raised $3.6 million to build robots that learn technician work by watching people do it, with first deployments aimed at early 2027.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: CoreWeave Beat Its Own Revenue Forecast, and Its Interest Bill Passed $846 Million in One Quarter
item.description: CoreWeave reported third-quarter results after Tuesday’s close. Revenue was $3.661 billion, up 168% from a year earlier and above the top of its own $3.45 billion to $3.60 billion guidance. Adjusted operating income was $379 million, against guidance of $200 million to $260 million. Net interest expense was $846 million, up from $310 million a year earlier, and the net loss was $709 million. Revenue backlog reached about $132.5 billion, and the company raised its full-year revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion.
item.content:encoded:
The quarter CoreWeave promised in this paper’s agenda arrived with both halves of the neocloud argument in the same filing. The operating half beat everything: revenue of $3.661 billion, up 168% year over year and 42% on the second quarter — the first quarter in which revenue grew by more than $1 billion — and adjusted operating income of $379 million, well above the $200 million to $260 million the company had guided. Adjusted EBITDA was $2.256 billion, a 62% margin. Backlog — contracted amounts not yet recognised as revenue, subject to delivery — reached about $132.5 billion, from $104.2 billion at the end of June. Active power doubled since the end of 2025 to 1.7 gigawatts.

The financing half is the same size as the operating half, and growing faster. Net interest expense was $846 million for the quarter, up from $310 million a year earlier and $640 million in the second quarter; the company guided to $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion for the fourth quarter. Against $207 million of GAAP operating income, the interest bill produced a net loss of $709 million. Total debt stood at $46.873 billion at September 30. Capital expenditure guidance for 2026 rose to $37 billion to $39 billion. Management raised the full-year revenue guide to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion and the exit run-rate target to $20 billion to $21 billion, and said the 2028 capacity it has brought to market is already sold out. The filing does not resolve the argument; it prices it. CoreWeave’s operations now earn real money at scale, and its lenders earn roughly four times as much from the same quarter.

item.title: Pines Planted Far From Home Grow Up to Four Times Faster, and Handle Drought Better
item.description: Across 192 sites on four continents, conifers planted in the Southern Hemisphere outgrew the same species at home — and stored more sugars and starches, a reserve that appears to carry them through dry spells.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: An Arctic Ocean Bacterium Appears to Live on Acetone and Carbon Dioxide
item.description: In the cold, food-scarce water of the Arctic Ocean, a bacterium appears to build what it needs to grow out of two unlikely ingredients: acetone, the chemical in nail-polish remover, and carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.
